newsitem.title: USA: Public aims for tax deadline, Congress for tax cut.
newsitem.headline: Public aims for tax deadline, Congress for tax cut.

text.p: As Americans around the country raced to meet the midnight tax filing deadline Tuesday, lawmakers popped up around every corner on Capitol Hill with remedies for relieving their stress.
Hundreds of post offices around the country were scheduled to stay open until midnight to allow the inevitable last-minute filers to meet the annual deadline.

At some locations mail handlers stood at curbside so people could drop off their tax returns and even buy stamps without getting out of their cars in a practice called "drive-by," a spokeswoman for the U.S. Postal Service said.
Meanwhile Democrats criticised Republicans who control Congress for missing the April 15 deadline by which Congress must formulate a budget blueprint.
Sen. Robert Kerrey, a Nebraska Democrat, suggested that Republican leaders fill out a form that taxpayers have to file when they miss the tax filing deadline.
Republicans held their own tax briefing down the hall to emphasise their commitment to cutting taxes this year.
Democrats said the taxes the Republicans wanted to cut would mainly help the wealthy at the expense of spending for programmes for the poor and elderly.

And everyone brought out charts -- big ones. Democrats had a blown-up April calendar with the 15th circled in red as the tax and budget deadline date. Republicans had huge bar charts showing that the tax burden on Americans had increased over the years.
According to President Clinton's budget proposal, $672.7 billion in individual income taxes and $176.2 billion in corporate income taxes were expected to be received this year.

The Internal Revenue Service, the tax collection agency which makes an easy political target because of the public's dislike for it, has been coming under fire for several weeks for snooping into taxpayers' returns and failing to upgrade its own computers.
On tax day, the agency came under virtual assault.

"Today April 15th is the appropriate day to emphasise first of all that the IRS is too big, too complicated, too out of control and needs to be changed in some very dramatic ways," said House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican.
The House was to vote on two tax-related bills Tuesday.
One bill, which had bipartisan support and was expected to pass, would create criminal penalties for IRS employees who snooped in taxpayer files.

Deputy Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers told a Senate subcommittee that unauthorised browsing of taxpayers' returns would not be tolerated and the IRS had been told to come up with a plan to stop it.

The second bill scheduled for a House vote was an amendment to the Constitution that would require a two-thirds vote of Congress to increase taxes except in times of war or national emergency. The amendment itself needed a two-thirds vote to pass, which appeared unlikely to occur.
Republicans who are seeking bigger tax cuts than the White House, pledged to reduce taxes this year.
"If there is a budget agreement between the White House and the Congress, it will include a tax component that will be significant," said House Republican Leader Dick Armey of Texas.

Senate Republican Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said he believed there would be a capital gains tax cut this year. Republicans also want a reduction in the tax on inheritances and tax relief for families.
But Senate Democratic Leader Tom Daschle of South Dakota said it was the wealthy the Republicans wanted to look after.

"They're (Republicans) holding hostage middle-class tax relief, Medicare reform, education investment, the environmental cleanup," Daschle said. "They're holding out for windfall tax breaks for the very wealthiest Americans who don't need them at all."
Republican and Democratic budget leaders were in negotiations with White House officials on the budget.
